article.overview: A regolith excavation instrument is a class of lunar surface tool or machine that digs, scoops, drives, drills or otherwise removes lunar regolith, the loose layer of dust, soil and broken rock that covers the Moon's bedrock. The catalogue entry is a generic class name rather than a single flown instrument. In the published record the term covers three kinds of hardware: (1) sampling devices that collect a small volume of soil or an intact core for laboratory analysis, such as hand scoops, driven core tubes and drills; (2) robotic excavators that move bulk regolith for construction or resource processing; and (3) laboratory prototypes and mission concepts. This article covers five examples. Three were flown on the Moon (Apollo 17 core tubes and deep drill, Luna 24 drill, Chang'e-5 drill and scoop), and one is a NASA excavator concept that has not flown (RASSOR). The examples are reported separately by status and must not be read as a universal specification for the class.
article.description: Lunar regolith is hard to excavate with conventional earthmoving methods. It is a fine, abrasive, electrostatically active dust that is mixed with rock fragments of many sizes, and it is found in a vacuum with large temperature swings. Published regolith tools therefore use a small number of approaches. Hand-operated sampling uses scoops, rakes and tubes that are driven or hammered into the ground, with the core kept in the tube. Automated sampling uses a drill or coring tool, often rotary-percussive, that either returns an intact core or a loose sample. Robotic excavation uses a bucket, scoop or drum mechanism on a mobile platform to move larger volumes. The key engineering problems across all of these are reaction forces at the tool and its mount, the difficulty of retaining a core in loose or layered material, keeping drill cuttings from jamming the mechanism, and sealing or protecting the sample for transfer to Earth or to a laboratory. Depth is an important performance measure because deeper material may preserve different layers, which can be a sampling goal in its own right.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: For sampling devices, the purpose is to obtain material that can be analysed in a laboratory. Depth-resolved cores can show how the regolith is layered and how its composition and exposure history change with depth. Yang and Lin (2020) note that drill cores from Chang'e-5 can help constrain space weathering, the set of processes that alter the surface of airless bodies through micrometeorite impacts and solar and cosmic radiation [3]. For robotic excavators, the purpose is to supply bulk regolith for construction or for in-situ resource utilisation. The NASA RASSOR concept describes regolith as feedstock for a separate plant that extracts oxygen [1]. These are design goals and mission concepts unless stated otherwise in the examples below.
article.operating_principle: Three operating principles recur in the sources reviewed. First, a hollow core tube is driven into the regolith by hammering or pushing, so that material fills the tube and is retained when it is withdrawn. The Apollo 17 double drive tube is described this way in the NASA sample-curation material reviewed in this run [no numbered reference; see data_quality_notes]. Second, a drill uses rotation and, in the Luna 24 and Chang'e-5 examples, percussion to cut a core. The Luna 24 description reports rotation alone to a set depth and then combined percussion and rotation [2]. The Chang'e-5 lander's coring drill is described as rotary-percussive [4]. Third, a robotic arm carries a scoop that acquires loose surface material and small rocks, as in the Chang'e-5 surface sampler [4]. The RASSOR concept is a mobile excavator whose drums or buckets move regolith in repeated trips [1]. Its detailed mechanism is not described in the note reviewed here.
article.scientific_importance: Excavation and sampling are central to lunar science because the regolith records the Moon's surface history. Depth-resolved samples allow scientists to compare surface and subsurface material, to study weathering and mixing, and to link surface spectra with laboratory measurements. Sample return gives laboratories direct access to material of known origin and depth, and the Apollo, Luna and Chang'e-5 samples have each been used in laboratory studies. For engineering, excavation data on cohesion, layering, rock content and drilling loads inform the design of future construction and resource-processing hardware. The importance of this class therefore depends on the specific tool. A passive scoop tells scientists about the top few centimetres, whereas a core that reaches metre depths can reveal stratigraphy. No single example should be treated as representative of the whole class.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, power or depth specification for a regolith excavation instrument. The entries below range from hand-operated tools with no published mass to a concept with a mass target. Where a value is given, it is tied to the exact hardware and source named in the example. Where no reliable value has been published, the text says so.

examples.name: Apollo 17 double drive tube (samples 73001 and 73002)
examples.status: Flown on the Moon (Apollo 17, December 1972); hand-operated by the crew
examples.summary: The Apollo 17 double drive tube was a pair of thin cylindrical sample-collection tubes. According to the NASA sample-curation page reviewed in this run, Apollo 17 astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt collected the regolith in December 1972 by hammering the tubes into a slide deposit in the Taurus-Littrow Valley. The lower half, 73001, was first vacuum sealed on the Moon and then stored in a second protective outer vacuum tube. The upper half, 73002, was returned in an unsealed container and was opened in 2019, according to the same page. The page states that 73001 was 'very full', as shown by CT scanning. The NASA page gives no tube diameter or length. A secondary summary gives a 4 cm diameter and 30 cm segments, but this has not been verified against a primary document and is not used here. The page does not give a station number. A separate attribution places the sample at Station 3, and this conflict is unresolved.
key_values: Status: flown, hand-operated by astronauts (December 1972). Power, mass and automation: not applicable.
Tube dimensions: not stated on the NASA page reviewed; a secondary summary gives 4 cm diameter (unverified).
Sample 73001: vacuum sealed on the Moon, opened under controlled conditions (NASA page reviewed in this run).
Sample 73002: returned unsealed and opened in 2019 (NASA page reviewed in this run).

examples.name: Apollo 17 deep drill core (sample series 70001 to 70009)
examples.summary: The Apollo 17 deep drill collected a long core of regolith in the Taurus-Littrow Valley. A search-result summary of NASA curation material reports a drill of about 3 m, a recovered core of about 290 cm, a core diameter of about 2 cm, a battery-powered rotary-percussion drive running at 280 rpm and 2270 blows per minute, and a collection point about 200 m west of the lunar module. These figures are not verified against the primary NASA PDF [5], which could not be parsed in this run. Recovery is reported as close to complete. The drill's power-supply and mass values were not found in primary text.
key_values: Status: flown on the Moon (Apollo 17). Operated by astronauts.
Drill length about 3 m and recovered core about 290 cm: reported in secondary summary of NASA material [5]; not verified.
Core diameter about 2 cm and drive speed 280 rpm, 2270 blows per minute: reported in secondary summary [5]; not verified.
Mass and power: not verified.

examples.name: Luna 24 soil drill (Soviet automated sample return, 1976)
examples.type: Automated rotary-percussion drill on a lander
examples.summary: Luna 24 carried an automated drill that returned a column of lunar soil to Earth. The Russian Space Web page reviewed in this run states a target of return of soil 'from the depth of up to 2.5 meters'. It reports rotation-only drilling to 120 cm, followed by combined percussion and rotation. The same page says the drill 'reached a depth of two meters under a 30-degree angle toward the local vertical' and also says it was 'penetrating 225 centimeters deep into the soil'. These two statements are not reconciled in the source. The returned soil mass is reported as 170.1 g, packed in a 160 cm column. The sample tube is reported as a 260 cm flexible tube of 12 mm diameter. A block of 'known specifications' for an 'LB-09' drill gives an outer diameter of 15 mm, an inner diameter of 8 mm, a length of 3157 mm and a drilling range of 2575 mm. The page does not say how this block relates to the drilling depth it reports. The source is secondary and has not been checked against the Soviet or Russian mission documentation.
key_values: Status: flown on the Moon (Luna 24, 1976), automated.
Target depth: up to 2.5 m (stated target, secondary source [2]).
Reported penetration: 225 cm; also reported as reaching 2 m at 30 degrees from vertical (internally inconsistent [2]).
Returned soil: 170.1 g, in a 160 cm column (secondary source [2]).
'LB-09' specification block: outer diameter 15 mm, inner diameter 8 mm, length 3157 mm, drilling range 2575 mm (relationship to the mission drill unclear [2]).
Mass and power: not verified in sources read.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 lander coring drill and surface scoop (2020)
examples.type: Rotary-percussive coring drill and robotic-arm scoop on a lander
examples.summary: The Chang'e-5 lander used two methods of sample collection. The first was a coring drill, and the second was a four-degree-of-freedom robotic arm with a scoop [3][4]. According to the eoportal mission overview, the coring drill was designed to acquire one or more intact cores of up to 2 m depth, using a rotary-percussive mechanism. The core was delivered to the ascent vehicle inside a Kevlar tube [4]. The eoportal page also says the lander 'began drilling for samples 2 meters below the surface', which conflicts with the design depth statement and is not resolved in the source. The planned split was about 0.5 kg from drilling and about 1.5 kg from scooping. The eoportal page reports a total of 1.731 kg returned, without a breakdown between drill and scoop [4]. Drilling is reported to have finished on 1 December 2020, and surface scooping to have finished on 2 December 2020 [4]. Yang and Lin describe the sample as soil core drilling plus scooping of soil and rock fragments [3]. The achieved drill depth has not been verified. A secondary search summary of a 2023 journal paper reports about 1 m, but that paper could not be accessed in this run (HTTP 403), so no achieved depth is stated here.
key_values: Status: flown on the Moon (Chang'e-5, December 2020).
Coring drill design: intact core up to 2 m, rotary-percussive mechanism (eoportal, design statement [4]).
Achieved drill depth: not verified in this run (a secondary summary reports about 1 m; primary paper not accessed).
Sampling split planned: about 0.5 kg drilling and 1.5 kg scooping [4].
Total returned: 1.731 kg, not broken down by method (eoportal [4]).
Surface arm: four degrees of freedom, with a scoop (eoportal [4]).
Mass and power of the drill and arm: not publicly specified in sources read.

examples.name: RASSOR (NASA Kennedy Space Center excavator concept)
examples.status: Concept and prototype development; not flown
examples.summary: The Regolith Advanced Surface Systems Operations Robot (RASSOR) is a NASA Kennedy Space Center concept for a lightweight robotic excavator. The 2015 NASA technical note describes it as 'a lightweight (<100 kg) robot' and frames the mass as a design target [1]. The note describes a trip cadence of '35 trips of 20 kg loads every 24 hours', which corresponds to about 700 kg of regolith per day. That daily figure is a derived calculation in this article, not a value stated in the note. The note describes a nominal mission of five years in which the robot delivers regolith feedstock to a separate chemical plant that extracts oxygen. With four units, the note says the concept 'would achieve 10 tonnes of oxygen per year' (8 t for rocket propellant and 2 t for life support) [1]. The status of this figure is conditional and concept-level. The note does not state that any unit has been built to this specification or flown. A later RASSOR 2.0 prototype value is reported in a search summary but was not verified against a primary NASA document, so it is not used here.
key_values: Status: concept/prototype, not flown.
Mass: design target of less than 100 kg (NASA note [1]); not a measured value.
Excavation cadence: 35 trips of 20 kg per 24 hours (NASA note [1]); the approximately 700 kg per day figure is derived here.
Nominal mission: five years; four units cited for 10 t oxygen per year (conditional concept statement [1]).
Dimensions and power: not stated in the note reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the class as a whole. Dimensions are available only for some examples, and these are given as reported by the cited source. The NASA note on RASSOR gives no dimensions [1]. The Luna 24 source reports tube and drill lengths, but it is not clear which assembly each figure refers to [2]. The Apollo 17 core-tube dimensions were not stated on the NASA page checked in this run.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for most examples. The RASSOR note gives a design target of 'a lightweight (<100 kg) robot' and describes this as a target rather than a measured mass [1]. No measured mass was found in the primary sources read for the Apollo 17 tools, the Luna 24 drill or the Chang'e-5 drill and scoop, so no value is given for them.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources read in this run. The Apollo 17 deep drill is reported in a secondary summary as battery-powered, which is not verified against the primary NASA document [5]. No power figure was found for the Luna 24 drill or the Chang'e-5 drill and scoop. The RASSOR note does not give a power figure [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Payload-specific environmental requirements for these examples were not found in the sources read. In general terms, a lunar surface excavation or sampling device has to operate in a vacuum, across large day-night temperature swings, in low gravity and in abrasive, electrostatically charged dust. These are general engineering conditions for the lunar surface rather than values from a cited source for any single instrument. Excavation in reduced gravity must also handle reaction forces at the tool and its mount; this is general engineering context and is not attributed to a specific source here. Mechanical behaviour of the regolith, such as cohesion, rock content and layering, is the main variable in drilling performance. Specific thermal, dust-tolerance, radiation and cycle-life qualification data were not publicly specified in the sources read.
article.limitations: This article describes a class with no single design. The examples are unevenly documented. The Apollo 17 and Chang'e-5 examples rely on NASA and eoportal pages, a secondary summary, and an unread primary paper. The Luna 24 example relies on a secondary web page with internal inconsistencies. The RASSOR example is a concept, and some of its figures are conditional. Depth, length and mass values differ between sources for the same hardware, and the reasons are not explained. Operating conditions, failure modes and qualification test data were not found for most examples. The Chang'e-5 achieved drill depth is not stated as verified.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Regolith excavation instruments reach the Moon in different ways depending on their type. Hand tools such as the Apollo 17 core tubes were carried by the crew and used during extravehicular activity. Automated drills and scoops, such as the Luna 24 and Chang'e-5 systems, are integrated with a lander that carries them through Earth integration, launch, transfer, descent and surface operation. A mobile excavator concept such as RASSOR would need stowage, release from a lander or rover, traverse and servicing. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted in this article, because verified interface evidence was not found.
transportation_process: Earth integration: the tool is mounted in the lander or on the crew equipment and checked against the spacecraft's mechanical, electrical and thermal interfaces.
Launch and lunar transfer: the tool travels stowed, with its power and thermal conditioning supplied by the carrier.
Landing and delivery: the lander carries the tool to the surface. For automated systems, the arm or drill is deployed from the lander.
Deployment and operation: the arm or drill is positioned, drives or drills, and collects the sample into a container or tube.

Sample handling: the core or scoop is sealed or stored for transfer to the ascent vehicle or the return capsule. Chang'e-5 used a Kevlar tube and sealed vacuum container for transfer to its ascent vehicle [4].
Return chain: for sample-return missions, the sample must survive ascent, transfer, return and curation. Constraints are discussed in the example sources but not quantified here.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment methods differ by example. The Apollo 17 core tubes were pushed or hammered into the regolith by astronauts [see the NASA curation material reviewed; no numbered reference]. The Luna 24 and Chang'e-5 drills were operated by the lander as automated sample systems [2][4]. The Chang'e-5 surface scoop was held by a four-degree-of-freedom arm [4]. RASSOR is a concept for a mobile robot that would move regolith over repeated trips [1]. Power, data and thermal interfaces for these systems are not publicly specified for the examples above.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 17 collected core tubes and a deep drill core in December 1972 [5]. Luna 24 returned soil from a drilled column in 1976 [2]. Chang'e-5 collected drill and scoop samples in December 2020 [3][4]. RASSOR is a concept and has no flight history [1].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any example in this article. The Chang'e-5 sampling system is compatible only with its own lander, as flown. The Apollo 17, Luna 24 and RASSOR interfaces to any other vehicle are not assessed. The transportation_compatibility_verified_for_specific_landers research flag remains false.

article.historical_significance: Lunar regolith excavation has a long history, beginning with the hand-driven core tubes and the deep drill core collected during Apollo 17 in December 1972 [5]. The Soviet Luna 24 mission returned soil collected by an automated drill in 1976 [2]. The Chang'e-5 mission in December 2020 combined a drill and a scoop for its sample return, and Yang and Lin note that its drill core is useful for studying space weathering [3]. The RASSOR concept reflects an effort to treat regolith as a resource for future surface operations [1]. The historical significance of each example depends on its status: the Apollo and Luna samples and the Chang'e-5 sample are physical records of flown hardware, and RASSOR is a design concept.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Several specific uncertainties are recorded here. (1) The Luna 24 source gives 225 cm and 2 m as penetration depths for the same drill without reconciliation [2]. (2) The Chang'e-5 eoportal page gives both a 2 m design depth and a statement that drilling began 2 m below the surface [4]. (3) The Chang'e-5 achieved drill depth is not verified; a secondary summary of an inaccessible 2023 paper reports about 1 m. (4) The Apollo 17 deep-drill figures come from a search summary of NASA material and were not verified against the primary PDF [5]. (5) The Apollo 17 double drive tube's station attribution conflicts between sources. (6) No direct image asset URL was verified for any example, so this article contains no embedded images. (7) No power, mass or environmental-qualification data were verified for the flown examples. (8) RASSOR figures are design targets or conditional concept values, not measured performance [1]. (9) The article does not use any values from other payloads in the catalogue.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue entry 95 is 'Regolith excavation instrument' in category 4, 'Subsurface exploration and drilling', per lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md. It is a generic class name, so no single hardware instance was assumed.

No direct image asset URL was verified for any example in this run. The image registry is empty and no images are embedded. The NASA Apollo 17 and eoportal pages were read for context; their image listings were not used as verified assets. The eoportal page lists a sampling-scoop sketch credited to the Harbin Institute of Technology, but its full URL was not verified and it was not used.

A NASA Apollo 17 double drive tube sample-curation page was read, but its canonical URL could not be determined. The only URL found contains a query string and reduces to the NASA homepage after cleanup, so it is not listed as a reference. Its facts are stated without a numbered citation.

The Apollo 17 double drive tube's tube diameter and length are not stated on the NASA page reviewed. A secondary summary gives 4 cm diameter and 30 cm segments; these are not verified and are not used.

The Apollo 17 deep-drill figures (about 3 m drill, about 290 cm core, 2 cm diameter, 280 rpm, 2270 blows per minute, battery power) come from a search-result summary of NASA material. The primary PDF was saved locally but could not be parsed in this run.
The Luna 24 source is secondary and internally inconsistent (225 cm versus reaching 2 m). Its 'LB-09' specification block is unexplained. Mass and power values for the Luna 24 drill were not found.

The Chang'e-5 IJRR-style drill paper (DOI 10.1177/02783649231187918) returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The secondary summary's 1 m achieved-depth figure is therefore unverified and is not stated as fact. The eoportal page also says drilling began 2 m below the surface, which conflicts with its design statement.

A RASSOR 2.0 mass of 66 kg and throughput of 2.7 t per day were seen only in a search summary of a conference paper and were not verified. They are not used in the article. The RASSOR figures used are from the NASA 2015 note only.
The 700 kg per day RASSOR figure is a derived calculation (35 trips of 20 kg in 24 hours), not a stated value.
General lunar-surface environmental conditions are described without a payload-specific source. No environmental qualification data were found for the examples.
No power, mass or dimension data were verified for the Apollo 17 double drive tube, the Chang'e-5 drill and scoop, or RASSOR beyond the design target.
Lunar landing-site and location recommendations are excluded at the user's request. Landing-location detail is not included in this article.
The progress ledger, catalogue and other payload files were not modified, per the run instructions. The progress-ledger update in the generator skill was not performed.
